newsitem.title: COMOROS: Heavy going for plane crash rescuers on Comoros.
newsitem.headline: Heavy going for plane crash rescuers on Comoros.

text.p: Rescuers said on Sunday they needed at least 36 hours and supplies of special equipment to recover bodies still trapped in the submerged wreckage of a hijacked Ethiopian airliner which crashed off the Comoro Islands.

Captain Bruno Beausse, commanding a team of 15 French rescue divers which flew in from the Indian Ocean island of Reunion on Sunday, said he would need heavy cutting equipment, underwater lighting and protective gear before recovery work could resume.
"We are operating in conditions of very great difficulty," Beausse told Reuters. "I have no intention of endangering my men's lives."

He said he and his divers had worked four hours underwater to recover just eight bodies from the wreckage of the Boeing 767 which crashed just offshore one of the Comoro Islands near the Le Galawa Beach resort on Saturday.

"The rest, somewhere between 50 and 70 I would estimate, are trapped in the wreckage. We've asked for heavy cutting equipment, the kind of tools you need to cut people from car wrecks, and we are expecting that to come from Reunion by tomorrow (Monday)," Beausse said.
But he said it would probably not be before low tide on Monday, that is about 8 p.m. (1700 GMT), that he could mount a sustained operation to recover the bodies.
He also noted that by that time there would be a problem of putrefaction, necessitating protective equipment for his divers.
"The weather conditions are good now but they could worsen at any time," Beausse added.
The plane was carrying 175 passengers and crew. At least 67 people died. Fifty-two survived, according to Ethiopian Airlines' main office in Addis Ababa.
The luxurious hotel complex with its palm-fringed, white-sand beach and turquoise sea has been cordoned off by police to assist rescue operations.

On the edge of the small bay, hundreds of villagers crowded to watch the dinghies go back and forth to the wreckage. Inside the complex tourists lounged around the pool deck and still more gathered on the beach to watch the proceedings. A subdued but calm atmosphere prevailed at the hotel.
The green, white-bordered tail of the plane was still stuck where it crashed several hundred metres (yards) away from the shore on Sunday afternoon, although the rest was submerged.

The white fuselage, in which most of the bodies are still believed to be trapped, has slowly been floating towards the hotel and had reached about 400 metres (450 yards) away from the beach by Sunday afternoon.
